questions.content:
Case study 1: Zandria's energy choices (10 marks)

Zandria is a small country with a fixed amount of land, labour and capital. Each year it can use these resources to build solar panels, wind turbines, or a mixture of the two. The table shows the maximum combinations it can produce (in thousands of units).

Option | Solar panels | Wind turbines
A | 0 | 60
B | 20 | 54
C | 40 | 42
D | 60 | 24
E | 80 | 0

(a) Define the term opportunity cost. (1 mark)
(b) Zandria moves from Option A to Option B. State the opportunity cost of the extra 20 thousand solar panels. (1 mark)
(c) Zandria moves from Option C to Option D. Calculate the opportunity cost of one extra thousand solar panels, in thousands of wind turbines. Show your working. (2 marks)
(d) The government announces a target of 60 thousand solar panels and 30 thousand wind turbines. Explain whether Zandria can reach this target with its current resources. (2 marks)
(e) State one change that could shift Zandria's production possibility curve outwards. (1 mark)
(f) Analyse why the opportunity cost of solar panels rises as Zandria produces more of them. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) The next best alternative given up (or the value of what is sacrificed) when a choice is made.
[1] (b) 6 thousand wind turbines (54 compared with 60).
[1] (c) Working: turbines lost = 42 - 24 = 18 for 20 extra panels, so 18 / 20.
[1] (c) Answer 0.9 thousand wind turbines per thousand panels.
[1] (d) At 60 thousand panels the maximum number of turbines is 24 thousand (Option D).
[1] (d) 30 thousand is more than 24 thousand, so the target is outside the curve and unattainable with current resources.
[1] (e) Any one: more or better resources, improved technology, more skilled labour, increased investment in capital.
[1] (f) Resources are not equally suited to both uses (they are specialised).
[1] (f) Moving more resources to panels means using resources that are better at making turbines.
[1] (f) So more and more turbines must be given up for each extra panel, shown by the rising opportunity cost in the table (0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2) - link to a bowed-out curve.
ECF: in (c) award the answer mark if the working uses the wrong pair of options but the division is correct and consistent. In (d) award the second mark for a consistent comparison with an incorrect value read from the table.
Common errors: giving 0.9 as a total rather than per thousand; dividing panels by turbines (giving 1.11); saying the target is achievable because the totals add to 90, which is less than the 140 reached by adding the two maximums; describing the shape of the curve without explaining why.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Case study 2: The rice market in Tello (12 marks)

The table shows the monthly market for rice in the country of Tello. Price is in dollars per kilogram and quantities are in thousands of tonnes.

Price per kg ($) | Quantity demanded | Quantity supplied
1 | 110 | 30
2 | 90 | 50
3 | 70 | 70
4 | 50 | 90
5 | 30 | 110
6 | 10 | 130

To lower food prices, the government gives rice farmers a subsidy. As a result, the quantity supplied rises by 40 thousand tonnes at every price. Demand does not change.

(a) Identify the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity before the subsidy. (2 marks)
(b) At a price of $5 per kg, calculate the surplus and explain what is likely to happen to the price. (2 marks)
(c) State the new equilibrium price and quantity after the subsidy. (2 marks)
(d) One million kilograms equals one thousand tonnes, so total spending by consumers in millions of dollars equals price multiplied by quantity. Calculate the change in total consumer spending on rice caused by the subsidy. (2 marks)
(e) Explain why a subsidy shifts the supply curve to the right. (2 marks)
(f) Explain one disadvantage of the subsidy for the government. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Equilibrium price $3 per kg.
[1] (a) Equilibrium quantity 70 thousand tonnes.
[1] (b) Surplus = 110 - 30 = 80 thousand tonnes.
[1] (b) Sellers hold unsold stock, so competition between them pushes the price down towards equilibrium.
[1] (c) New equilibrium price $2 per kg (new supply 50 + 40 = 90 equals demand of 90).
[1] (c) New equilibrium quantity 90 thousand tonnes.
[1] (d) Before: 3 x 70 = 210 and after: 2 x 90 = 180 (million dollars).
[1] (d) Change = 180 - 210 = a fall of $30 million.
[1] (e) A subsidy is money paid to producers that lowers their costs of production.
[1] (e) Producers are willing and able to supply more at each price, so supply increases (shifts right).
[1] (f) The government must pay for the subsidy (an opportunity cost) using tax revenue or borrowing.
[1] (f) Development of the point: that money cannot be spent on other services such as schools or hospitals, or the subsidy may keep inefficient farms in business.
ECF: in (c) and (d) follow through from an incorrect equilibrium in (a) or an incorrect reading of the new schedule if the method is consistent. Allow a total in (d) given as a decrease of 30 without a unit if the calculation is shown.
Common errors: shifting supply left; stating the surplus as 110 or 30; confusing the change in quantity (20) with the change in spending; writing only that the subsidy is expensive without saying who pays or what is given up.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Case study 3: Brightway Bikes (12 marks)

Brightway Bikes sells electric bicycles in the city of Kirel. The firm raised the price of its most popular model from $400 to $440. Monthly sales fell from 1,000 bicycles to 850 bicycles.

Price elasticity of demand (PED) = percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
Income elasticity of demand (YED) = percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in income.
Price elasticity of supply (PES) = percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.

(a) Calculate the percentage change in price. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the percentage change in quantity demanded. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the price elasticity of demand. (1 mark)
(d) State whether demand is elastic or inelastic and give a reason. (1 mark)
(e) Calculate the change in Brightway's monthly revenue after the price rise. Show your working. (2 marks)
(f) Use your answers to explain what would happen to the firm's revenue if it lowered the price. (2 marks)
(g) When average incomes in Kirel rise by 5%, demand for the bicycles rises by 8%, while demand for bus tickets falls by 2%. Calculate the YED for the bicycles and the bus tickets and state the type of good each represents. (2 marks)
(h) If a 10% rise in the price of bicycles causes the quantity supplied to rise by 4%, calculate the PES and explain what this value shows. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) +10%.
[1] (b) -15%.
[1] (c) PED = -15 / 10 = -1.5 (accept 1.5).
[1] (d) Elastic, because the value is greater than 1 in size (the quantity falls by a bigger percentage than the price rises).
[1] (e) Working: revenue before = 400 x 1,000 = $400,000 and after = 440 x 850 = $374,000.
[1] (e) Change = a fall of $26,000 per month.
[1] (f) Demand is elastic, so a price cut causes a bigger percentage rise in quantity than the fall in price.
[1] (f) Therefore total revenue would rise.
[1] (g) Bicycles YED = 8 / 5 = 1.6 (a normal good, and a luxury because above 1).
[1] (g) Bus tickets YED = -2 / 5 = -0.4 (an inferior good).
[1] (h) PES = 4 / 10 = 0.4.
[1] (h) Supply is inelastic: producers cannot raise output quickly when price changes (for example because of limited capacity or time needed to make bikes).
ECF: if the price change in (a) is wrong, follow through into (c) and (e) if the method is correct. Allow a PED quoted with a negative sign or as a positive number.
Common errors: dividing the change in price by the change in quantity (giving 0.67); using the new figure as the denominator in percentage change; stating that revenue fell in (f) because quantity fell; calling a negative YED a normal good.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Case study 4: The economy of Marnovia (12 marks)

The table shows the expenditure data for Marnovia (billions of dollars). The general price level index was 100 in 2023 and 104 in 2024. Marnovia's population in 2024 was 47 million.

Component | 2023 | 2024
Consumption (C) | 520 | 560
Investment (I) | 160 | 150
Government spending (G) | 190 | 200
Exports (X) | 210 | 230
Imports (M) | 180 | 200

GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)

(a) Calculate Marnovia's GDP for 2023. Show your working. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate Marnovia's GDP for 2024. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the percentage growth in nominal GDP between 2023 and 2024, to two decimal places. (2 marks)
(d) Calculate real GDP for 2024 in 2023 prices, to one decimal place. (2 marks)
(e) Calculate GDP per capita for 2024, in dollars. (1 mark)
(f) Explain why real GDP gives a better measure of economic growth than nominal GDP. (2 marks)
(g) Explain one limitation of GDP per capita as a measure of living standards. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Working: 520 + 160 + 190 + (210 - 180).
[1] (a) GDP 2023 = 900 billion dollars.
[1] (b) GDP 2024 = 560 + 150 + 200 + (230 - 200) = 940 billion dollars.
[1] (c) Working: (940 - 900) / 900 x 100.
[1] (c) 4.44%.
[1] (d) Working: 940 / 104 x 100 (or 940 / 1.04).
[1] (d) 903.8 billion dollars.
[1] (e) 940 billion / 47 million = $20,000.
[1] (f) Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, so it can rise only because prices have risen.
[1] (f) Real GDP removes the effect of inflation so it shows the change in the quantity of goods and services produced (here growth of only about 0.43%).
[1] (g) It is an average, so it hides inequality in how income is shared (or ignores unpaid work, the informal economy, the environment, health or leisure).
[1] (g) So a high GDP per capita does not guarantee that most people enjoy a high standard of living - a developed explanation with an example.
ECF: carry an incorrect 2023 or 2024 GDP forward into (c), (d) and (e) if the method is correct. In (d) accept 903.85 and 904.
Common errors: adding imports instead of subtracting them (giving 1,260 and 1,340 for the two years); dividing by 1.04 for 2023; forgetting to convert billions and millions in (e); using GDP per capita as total GDP divided by 47 without units.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Case study 5: Prices and jobs in Veldara (12 marks)

Veldara's statistics office measures inflation using a basket of goods and services. The 2023 index for every item is 100. The table shows the weight of each category in the basket and its price index in 2024.

Category | Weight (%) | Price index 2024
Food | 40 | 110
Housing | 30 | 104
Transport | 20 | 95
Other goods and services | 10 | 102

In 2024 Veldara had a labour force of 8.0 million people, of whom 0.44 million were unemployed. Average money wages rose by 3% between 2023 and 2024.

(a) Define inflation. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the weighted price index for 2024. Show your working. (2 marks)
(c) State the rate of inflation between 2023 and 2024. (1 mark)
(d) Calculate the unemployment rate in 2024. (2 marks)
(e) State whether real wages rose or fell and calculate the approximate change in real wages. (2 marks)
(f) Explain one cost of high inflation for households. (2 marks)
(g) Explain one cause of cyclical unemployment. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) A sustained (continuing) rise in the general price level.
[1] (b) Working: (0.40 x 110) + (0.30 x 104) + (0.20 x 95) + (0.10 x 102).
[1] (b) 44 + 31.2 + 19 + 10.2 = 104.4.
[1] (c) 4.4%.
[1] (d) Working: 0.44 / 8.0 x 100.
[1] (d) 5.5%.
[1] (e) Real wages fell, because wages rose by 3% but prices rose by 4.4%.
[1] (e) Approximate change = 3 - 4.4 = about -1.4% (accept -1.3% from the exact calculation 1.03 / 1.044).
[1] (f) Purchasing power falls: money buys fewer goods (especially if incomes do not keep up), or savings lose value.
[1] (f) Developed point such as the cost to households on fixed incomes, or uncertainty making budgeting difficult.
[1] (g) Cyclical unemployment is linked to a fall in total demand during a downturn (recession).
[1] (g) Firms sell less, so they cut output and workers - an explained chain of cause and effect.
ECF: follow through the weighted index from (b) into (c). In (e) allow the fall or rise judgement to follow an incorrect inflation figure from (c) if consistent.
Common errors: using a simple average of the four indices (giving 102.75); stating the index 104.4 as the inflation rate; dividing unemployed by the whole population or by the number employed; stating that real wages rose because the money wage rose.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Case study 6: A sugar tax on Corvale (14 marks)

The government of Corvale introduced a tax of $0.30 on every bottle of fizzy drink to reduce sugar consumption. Producers passed all the tax on to consumers, so the price rose from $1.50 to $1.80. Annual sales fell from 100 million bottles to 85 million bottles.

The health ministry estimates that diseases linked to sugar cost the health service $400 million a year. It predicts that the tax will reduce this cost by 2%. The government plans to spend the tax revenue on free school meals. Critics say lower-income households spend a larger share of their income on fizzy drinks, and that some shoppers will buy cheaper sugary drinks from across the border. Alternatives include a ban on advertising to children and subsidies for fruit and vegetables.

(a) Calculate the price elasticity of demand for fizzy drinks. Show your working. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the annual revenue from the tax. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the change in the producers' annual revenue, excluding the tax, after the tax was introduced. (2 marks)
(d) Explain why governments tax goods that cause negative externalities. (2 marks)
(e) Evaluate the effectiveness of the sugar tax as a policy to improve public health in Corvale. (7 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Working: price change = +20% and quantity change = -15%.
[1] (a) PED = -15 / 20 = -0.75 (inelastic; accept 0.75).
[1] (b) Revenue = 0.30 x 85 million = $25.5 million.
[1] (c) Producers' revenue before = 1.50 x 100 million = $150 million; after = 1.50 x 85 million = $127.5 million.
[1] (c) Change = a fall of $22.5 million.
[1] (d) A negative externality is a cost imposed on third parties (here the health service and society) that the buyer and seller do not pay.
[1] (d) A tax raises the price so that it includes the external cost, reducing consumption towards the socially efficient level.
Evaluation (7 marks), indicative content - award up to 7 for points such as the following, with a maximum of 4 for one-sided answers and a maximum of 5 without a justified conclusion:
[1] (e) For: consumption fell by 15 million bottles (15%), so the policy reduces sugar intake.
[1] (e) For: the demand is inelastic (0.75), so the tax raises substantial revenue ($25.5 million) as well as reducing use.
[1] (e) For: predicted health savings of 2% of $400 million = $8 million a year (calculation shown or used).
[1] (e) Against: the savings of $8 million are much smaller than the revenue, and the 15% fall is modest, so the tax does not remove the problem; demand is inelastic so the tax is not very effective at cutting consumption.
[1] (e) Against: regressive effect on lower-income households and cross-border buying that weakens the effect.
[1] (e) Alternatives such as an advertising ban or fruit subsidies might work alongside or instead; the effects depend on the time scale (habits change slowly) and on how the revenue is used (school meals can add a health benefit).
[1] (e) A justified judgement (for example, partly effective: useful as one part of a package) that is linked to the evidence.
ECF: follow through from an incorrect elasticity in (a) when evaluating whether demand is elastic or inelastic. In (c) allow the change given as a percentage (-15%) only if the dollar value is shown.
Common errors: including the tax in producer revenue (giving a rise to $153 million); dividing the quantity change by the dollar change in price; evaluating with no reference to the data; listing advantages and disadvantages without any judgement.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Case study 7: Pelmar's trade (12 marks)

Pelmar exports coffee and imports mobile phones. The world price of a phone is $500. To protect its new phone assembly industry, Pelmar's government puts a 20% tariff on imported phones. After the tariff, Pelmar still imports 300,000 phones a year.

Pelmar's currency is the crown. Pelmar sells coffee for 2,400 crowns per tonne. Its buyers in the country of Zeta pay in Zeta dollars. At first the exchange rate was 1 crown = 0.80 Zeta dollars. Later the crown appreciated to 1 crown = 0.90 Zeta dollars.

(a) Define the term tariff. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the price of an imported phone in Pelmar after the tariff. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the government's annual revenue from the tariff. Show your working. (2 marks)
(d) Explain how a tariff can protect domestic producers. (2 marks)
(e) Calculate the price of one tonne of Pelmar coffee in Zeta dollars before and after the appreciation of the crown. (2 marks)
(f) Explain the likely effect of the appreciation on Pelmar's coffee exports. (2 marks)
(g) State two other types of trade barrier. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) A tax on imported goods.
[1] (b) $500 x 1.20 = $600.
[1] (c) Working: tariff per phone = $100.
[1] (c) 100 x 300,000 = $30 million.
[1] (d) The tariff raises the price of imports (to $600), making foreign phones more expensive.
[1] (d) Domestic phones become relatively cheaper, so consumers switch to them and local firms sell more.
[1] (e) Before: 2,400 x 0.80 = 1,920 Zeta dollars.
[1] (e) After: 2,400 x 0.90 = 2,160 Zeta dollars.
[1] (f) The coffee costs about 12.5% more for buyers in Zeta (1,920 to 2,160).
[1] (f) If demand is elastic, buyers will buy less, so exports fall (and may be replaced by coffee from other countries).
[1] (g) One mark each for two from: quotas, subsidies to domestic producers, embargoes, strict product standards or regulations, administrative delays. (Do not accept tariffs.)
[1] (g) Second distinct barrier.
ECF: follow through an incorrect tariff price from (b) into (c). Award (f) marks if the direction of the effect is consistent with a correct calculation in (e).
Common errors: adding 20 dollars instead of 20%; saying the tariff revenue is paid by the foreign exporter; saying that appreciation makes exports cheaper; confusing an appreciation with a depreciation.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Case study 8: Comparing Aldovia and Borneth (10 marks)

The table compares two countries.

Indicator | Aldovia | Borneth
GDP per capita (dollars) | 4,200 | 12,600
Life expectancy (years) | 64 | 76
Adult literacy rate (%) | 71 | 96
Infant deaths per 1,000 births | 48 | 9
Internet users (% of population) | 35 | 82

(a) Calculate how many times larger Borneth's GDP per capita is than Aldovia's. (1 mark)
(b) Compare the level of development of Aldovia and Borneth, using at least three indicators from the table. Use clear comparative language and include figures. (4 marks)
(c) Explain why GDP per capita alone is not a sufficient measure of a country's development. (2 marks)
(d) Explain one way in which foreign direct investment could help Aldovia to develop. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) 12,600 / 4,200 = 3 times.
Part (b) - 4 marks. Award one mark for each of up to three accurate comparisons that use data from the table, and one mark for communication.
[1] (b) A correct comparison using figures, for example: Borneth's life expectancy is 12 years higher (76 compared with 64).
[1] (b) A second correct comparison using figures, for example: Aldovia has an infant mortality rate of 48 per 1,000, which is 39 more than Borneth's 9 per 1,000.
[1] (b) A third correct comparison using figures, for example: 96% of Borneth's adults are literate, whereas only 71% are in Aldovia (or internet use 82% against 35%).
[1] (b) Communication: the answer is organised, uses comparative words (higher than, whereas, in contrast) and reaches a clear overall statement that Borneth is more developed on every indicator.
[1] (c) GDP per capita measures only average income (and not how it is shared).
[1] (c) Development also includes health, education and quality of life (such as life expectancy and literacy), so other indicators such as the Human Development Index are needed.
[1] (d) FDI means a foreign firm builds or buys business assets in Aldovia.
[1] (d) It creates jobs and incomes (or transfers technology and skills, or improves infrastructure).
[1] (d) Linked consequence: higher incomes and tax revenue can be spent on health and education, which raises living standards (any developed chain).
ECF: in (b) accept a comparison with a calculation error if the direction of the comparison is correct and a figure is quoted for both countries.
Common errors: quoting the figures without comparing them; describing only one country; saying that high GDP per capita means that all citizens are rich; stating that infant mortality is higher in Borneth.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Case study 9: Aldovia's economic strategy (16 marks)

Aldovia (population 7 million, see Case study 8) has a GDP of $29.4 billion. Its unemployment rate is 14%, inflation is 9% and average annual economic growth over the last five years was 3.1%. The government has borrowed to cover its budget deficits: public debt is $18 billion, on which it pays 5% interest a year. The government's annual budget is $6 billion. Spending on education is only 2.8% of GDP.

Two strategies are being debated.

Strategy 1: Spend more on education and health, paid for by further borrowing. Supporters say that a healthier and better educated workforce will become more productive and attract foreign investment.

Strategy 2: Focus on exports by lowering taxes on firms, reducing barriers to trade and allowing the currency to fall in value. Supporters say this will create jobs quickly. Critics say it makes imports more expensive and leaves the country dependent on a few export products, such as copper, whose world price changes a lot.

(a) Calculate public debt as a percentage of GDP, to one decimal place. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the annual interest Aldovia pays on its public debt. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the interest payment as a percentage of the government's annual budget. (1 mark)
(d) To what extent should Aldovia prioritise spending on education and health rather than an export-led strategy? Use the information above and your own knowledge. (13 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) 18 / 29.4 x 100 = 61.2%.
[1] (b) 5% of $18 billion = $0.9 billion (accept $900 million).
[1] (c) 0.9 / 6 x 100 = 15%.
Part (d) - indicative content. Award up to 13 marks across the following. A one-sided answer cannot score more than 9 marks and an answer without a judgement supported by evidence cannot score more than 10 marks.
[1] (d) Education and health raise human capital and productivity, increasing the productive capacity of the economy in the long run (shifting the PPC outwards).
[1] (d) Education spending of 2.8% of GDP is low, and the comparison with Borneth (literacy 71% against 96%, life expectancy 64 against 76 years) shows scope for improvement.
[1] (d) Better skills attract foreign direct investment and help reduce structural unemployment (14%) over time.
[1] (d) Developed analysis of the causal chain (spending - healthier, better educated workers - higher productivity and incomes - more tax revenue - lower deficits in the long term).
[1] (d) Counter-argument: public debt already stands at 61.2% of GDP and interest takes 15% of the budget, so more borrowing could crowd out other spending or cause worries among lenders.
[1] (d) The benefits of education take years to appear, whereas unemployment of 14% is a current problem.
[1] (d) Export strategy: lower costs and a weaker currency make exports cheaper, so demand and jobs can rise quickly.
[1] (d) Export strategy: a weaker currency raises import prices and could worsen inflation (already 9%), harming households; heavy reliance on a few products leaves the economy vulnerable to price changes.
[1] (d) Use of data from the case study in the argument (at least two pieces of accurate data are applied, not merely quoted).
[1] (d) Recognises that the strategies are not mutually exclusive, for example a mix with trade measures for jobs now and targeted education spending for growth later, and considers priorities such as the time scale and financing.
[1] (d) A clear judgement that answers 'to what extent' (for example, education and health should have priority only if financing is sustainable).
[1] (d) The judgement is justified with reference to criteria such as sustainability, time scale, equity or risk.
[1] (d) Clear, well-structured writing using economic terminology accurately (for example, productivity, human capital, comparative advantage, depreciation).
ECF: follow through an incorrect value from (a) to (c) when it is used correctly in the evaluation. Accept any reasoned conclusion that is supported by evidence.
Common errors: choosing a strategy without weighing the other; copying statistics from the case study with no analysis; using the same argument twice; calculating interest on GDP rather than debt (giving $1.47 billion); concluding with a statement that repeats the question.
Accept other valid points.
